chapter: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
title: Influences: Ellington and Fletcher Henderson
summary: Durham says Ellington influenced him most, with Henderson keeping jazz as dance music, and he now sees Ellington as 50 years ahead.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, when -- while you were doing these various things, I take it that you're hearing records all this time. I mean, who sort of influenced you during this period?

Mostly, my influence come from a guy like Duke Ellington. Sounded like he had something, you know, music and creating. And Fletcher Henderson, he (inaudible) another type of challenge. He had another type of thing going. But Duke Ellington he had a tone. See, like, now, some of my features on the guitar right now is In My Solitude. And things like that. I'm doing all that on the guitar.
The 12-string. But nobody would believe I played it, but I wouldn't play that around here, because
the way I'm playing it, you ain't going to be able to play it. And I had to get up on it out there, so --
When you sort of listen to the old records now, you can see where sort of Fletcher's idea was -- he really stayed with the conception of jazz as dance music.
Now, Duke is going out to --
Yeah, and, too, a more of a kind of concert conception, really.
Yeah. The more I listen to Duke now, the more I find out that he's much greater than any musician anybody -- in that band that anybody would ever realize, that even the guys in the band don't know.

They didn't even know it. Now, I begin to really find out what's happening, since so much has went under my head now, all the way down, and it's filed over, and Duke Ellington was so far gone then. He must have been 50 years ahead of his time with that style of music. And today --
